publications.title: Schedules for pick-and-place robots
publications.abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    The efficiency of pick-and-place robots that put parts into boxes relies on efficient schedules, which determine the order in which parts are picked. The scheduling problem can be formulated as an integer linear program (ILP). However, the resulting ILP cannot be solved for realistic scenarios. Therefore, approximate solution techniques based on local search heuristics and simplified ILPs are introduced. It will be shown that ILP-based solutions outperform search heuristics in terms of solution times and solution quality. Additionally, we consider an extended version of the pick-and-place robot with two arms. It is shown that the resulting scheduling problem can be handled similarly to the problem for the robot with one arm, but the number of variables in the resulting ILP increases from
                    
                      
                        $$O(P^3)$$
                        
                          
                            O
                            (
                            
                              P
                              3
                            
                            )
                          
                        
                      
                    
                    for one arm to
                    
                      
                        $$O(P^6)$$
                        
                          
                            O
                            (
                            
                              P
                              6
                            
                            )
                          
                        
                      
                    
                    for two arms, where
                    P
                    is the number of parts to be picked. Consequently, decomposition-based approaches are introduced that reduce the scheduling problem for two arms to several problems with one arm.

publications.title: Co-design As Collaborative Research
publications.abstract: Theodore Zamenopoulos and Katerina Alexiou discuss the field of co-design and its underpinning theories and methods. They argue that Design as a process is always concerned with addressing a challenge or opportunity to create a better future reality, and explore how co-design has evolved as a process of ensuring that those with the life experiences, expertise and knowledge are actively involved in these making new tools, products and services. They observe how the participatory turn in this field has been concerned with both changing the objects of design – whether this is services or objects – and with the changing processes of designing itself. They highlight four major traditions and their distinctive approaches, before exploring the politics and practices of co-design through case studies of work.

publications.title: Development of a Web-Based Correspondence Service Information System to Improve the Administrative Efficiency of Wonowoso Village
publications.abstract: Correspondence administration in Wonowoso Village relied on conventional procedures that lacked an integrated digital workflow for citizen submissions and administrative records. This study aimed to develop a web-based correspondence service information system to support more orderly village administration. Development comprised requirements mapping, system design, implementation, and functional verification. The application was built using Node.js, Express.js, EJS, MongoDB, and Mongoose, with Multer, express-session, bcryptjs, and Nodemailer supporting document uploads, administrator sessions, password security, and rejection notifications, respectively. Verification combined source-code inspection, desktop interface rendering, and examination of a MongoDB backup snapshot. The developed system provides four service types and connects citizen submissions with administrator processing through Pending, Approved, and Rejected statuses. Citizens can review service requirements, complete application forms, and upload supporting documents, while administrators can examine applications, assign letter numbers, preview letters, approve requests, and record reasons for rejection. The database snapshot contained four applications: one Approved and three Rejected. The system supports a more organized administrative workflow through centralized records, online submissions, and structured status management. Its contribution to administrative efficiency is therefore limited to workflow-level support; quantitative improvements were not established because pre–post service-time measurements and user usability testing were unavailable. The study provides a practical basis for refining digital village services and conducting broader field evaluations of efficiency and usability.

publications.title: STUDENTS’ PERSPECTIVES AND SIGNIFICANCE OF “WRITE AND IMPROVE” WEB APP
publications.abstract: This research study focuses on the pedagogical importance and student perspectives of the AI-driven “Write & Improve” web app in developing English writing skills. Using a mixed-methods research design, the study followed 24 students from the 12th grade at Mandakh Lyceum high school during a five-week experimental period. The quantitative results, gathered from a 5-point Likert scale survey, showed that 75% of the participants highly valued the web app because it provides immediate feedback on their work. However, there was a noticeable gap in how students understood this feedback, as 50-75% of them felt neutral about whether the automated suggestions were clear or detailed enough. At the same time, qualitative findings from focus group interviews and teacher observations showed a clear shift toward self-regulated learning. These results suggest that while the W&I web app effectively helps students practice a “Plan-Draft-Revise” cycle and reduces writing anxiety, its educational impact is most effective when combined with traditional teaching. The study concludes that the web app should not be seen as a standalone replacement for a teacher, but rather as a powerful supporting tool within a structured classroom environment. Ultimately, integrating this AI technology allows for a more active and repetitive approach to writing, helping students bridge the gap between receiving basic corrections and achieving true academic progress.

publications.title: International Journal of Web Services Research
publications.abstract: This paper investigates the problem of reputation management in composite services. The authors propose a novel reputation propagation technique in composite services. The proposed approach provides a fair distribution of reputation values so that a component service is neither penalised nor awarded for the poor and good performance, respectively, of other peer component services. Experiment results indicate that the proposed technique propagates the 'fair share' of reputation from the composite service to its component services.

publications.title: The AI Written RFP: what five engines tell buyers to require in fourteen software categories
publications.abstract: First public research release covering all 14 software categories: 2,003 criteria, 10,547 requirement spans, 2,417 explicit criterion and vendor associations, and 10,015 vendor page comparisons. The derived answer base is 2,093. Research completion and publication checks pass. Team review: in progress. Zero statements are represented as analyst verified. No synthetic captures or reviewer identities are included. This release includes the complete data tables, a 30-page report, the independent verifier and SHA256 integrity manifest. Source answers were captured on 22 to 23 Sep 2026 under method v1.1 and remain deposited at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22907695. Perplexity quotation text is omitted; exact source identifiers, offsets and hashes remain for verification. Every figure comes from the published method, v1.1. https://broadcastwell.com/methodology CC BY 4.0. Any named company may request one no-cost re-run at index@broadcastwell.com; both results are published.

publications.title: A Systematic Overview on AI Music Generation, Arrangement, and Orchestration
publications.abstract: The rapid growth of AI-based music generation, arrangement, and orchestration has resulted in a large and fragmented body of literature, making it increasingly difficult for researchers and practitioners to navigate recent developments and identify the most promising approaches. Existing surveys often focus on specific subfields or do not fully reflect recent advances such as diffusion models, transformer-based architectures, and large-scale commercial systems. This thesis addresses these gaps through a systematic literature review reported with reference to the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, investigating AI methods for music generation, arrangement, and orchestration published between 2020 and 2025. From 4,521 records identified across six academic sources, 1,083 could be exported to Zotero for record management and screening; after deduplication and eligibility assessment, 107 primary studies were included in the review. For each included study, information regarding methodology, datasets, musical representations, evaluation procedures, performance metrics, and code availability was extracted and organised in a comprehensive comparison table. The review extends the taxonomy proposed by Zhu et al. (2023), synthesises eight major research trends, and identifies and justifies 27 systems for in-depth analysis, whose available demonstrations and outputs are examined through a pilot exploratory listening analysis, and whose author-reported evaluations are synthesised separately. The contributions include an updated taxonomy of AI music systems, a structured comparison of 107 studies, a trend analysis spanning 2020–2025, and practical recommendations for future research in AI-assisted music generation, arrangement, and orchestration.

publications.title: Modeling collective action in POM: The Strategy–Operations–People framework
publications.abstract:
While many business situations relevant to production and operations management (POM), such as supply chain coordination or sustainable operations, involve some form of collective action; managerial frameworks for collective action rarely appear in POM contexts. Valuable insights may thus be missed, reducing the effectiveness and implementability of the proposed POM solutions. To bridge this gap, this paper presents a framework for collective action that has its roots in the organizational behavior literature. We formalize it mathematically not only to offer definitional clarity, but also to relate it to common POM modeling approaches. We then illustrate its relevance to POM by mapping it to case studies in supply chain coordination and sustainable operations. The proposed framework, named the Strategy–Operations–People (SOP) framework, is structured in three levels, comprising three elements, two elements, and one element, respectively. First, the
                    Strategy
                    level induces and enforces solidarity among all team members by specifying common goals, shared values, and well-defined rules. Second, the
                    Operations
                    level organizes the decentralized execution of collective action in autonomous subgroups through a detailed specification of roles and processes. Third, the
                    People
                    level requires the individual commitment of all team members to the proposed collective action program, since a team’s performance rests on the individual contributions of its members. The framework thus addresses the common, subgroup, and individual dimensions of collective action. The SOP framework also contributes to the broader fields of team leadership and organizational behavior in two ways. First, its mathematical formalization brings operational clarity on the defining scope of the framework’s elements. Second, mapping the framework to two problems in supply chain management and sustainable operations illustrates its broad applicability, moving beyond collective action within organizations, to guide collective action taking place across organizations.

publications.title: Disagreement-aware diagnosis of curriculum knowledge graphs in education with traceable interpretation changes: Data and code
publications.abstract: This dataset contains the research data, computational results, and source code supporting the study "Disagreement-aware diagnosis of curriculum knowledge graphs in education with traceable interpretation changes." The main collection comprises 30 historical MIT OpenCourseWare courses, 300 assessment tasks, 180 study-defined curriculum targets, 362 capability atoms, and 21,720 recorded judgments across six semantic mappings. ESM_1.zip contains source and version records, historical audit corrections, case-level evidence, adequacy classifications, paired minimum-change results, and computational verification records. ESM_2.zip contains the frozen curriculum data, recorded interpretations, provenance graphs, diagnostic queries, minimum-change witnesses, numerical results, and executable Python code. The numerical analyses can be reproduced from the archived judgments. Original third-party course documents are identified through source records rather than redistributed. The recorded semantic interpretations have not been independently adjudicated by human experts.

publications.title: Early-Stage Prediction of Open-Source Software Project Performance: Reproducibility Materials
publications.abstract: This repository provides the reproducibility materials associated with the study “Early-Stage Prediction of Open-Source Software Project Performance.” The study evaluates the outcome-conditional predictive value of early-stage repository signals across three dimensions of future OSS project performance: popularity, operational performance, and long-term sustainability. It uses repositories sampled from the npm, PyPI, Maven Central, and crates.io ecosystems and evaluates 30-, 90-, and 180-day observation windows (W30, W90, and W180). Model and hyperparameter selection was conducted using the 2015–2021 development period, while the 2022–2023 cohorts were reserved for locked final out-of-sample evaluation. The archived materials are intended to document the study’s analytical workflow, model-development protocol, frozen model specifications, evaluation procedures, and supporting reproducibility information. The contents of this archive should be interpreted together with the associated manuscript and its supplementary materials. The archive includes the historical feature-engineering and outcome-construction scripts, the final repository sample, frozen model-performance summaries, SHAP global-importance outputs for Y1, Y2, and Y3, and model-freeze and provenance recovery records. The archived materials document the analytical workflow and reported results; complete end-to-end reproducibility may additionally depend on the availability of the original GitHub event data and the computational environment. Licensing and Data Provenance The MIT License applies to the original Python scripts authored for this study. The Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0) license applies to the original research-generated summaries, documentation, and analytical outputs to the extent that the authors hold the necessary rights. The repository sample manifest contains publicly accessible GitHub repository identifiers and metadata. These identifiers remain attributable to their respective sources. Neither license grants additional rights over third-party content or overrides applicable source-platform terms. The archive does not include raw GitHub event histories, commit messages, or contributor email addresses. Reproduction of the complete analytical workflow may require additional upstream data and computational dependencies.
